steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing spherical cap harmonic analysis (SCHA) to characterise the morphology of rough, open surface patches. Motivate it from granular mechanics and engineering, give example applications, outline the method, and end with the paper's structure.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation: granular materials, numerical models, structural engineering
- Separating shape and roughness; spherical harmonics and their limit for open surfaces
- Proposal: SCHA, and example problems where it is useful
- What the SCHA method offers
- New conformal parameterisation onto a spherical cap
- Paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - granular mechanics (e.g. soil mechanics): particle interactions under various loading; shape, size, material properties vary widely
  - numerical models used to study how particle morphology and microstructures influence mechanical behaviour
  - similar in structural engineering: microstructure of concrete aggregates, stones in stone masonry; shape and roughness affect the matrices

- Shape vs roughness
  - need to model randomly shaped closed objects and their interactions
  - shape: finite/discrete element mesh; roughness: surface interaction laws, e.g. friction models
  - separating "shape" and "roughness" is challenging, but helps understand constitutive laws
  - recent decades: spherical harmonics (SH) analysis for shape/roughness of stones, aggregates
  - transformative for closed objects, hard for nominally flat, open surfaces (topological disks, free edges)

- Proposal: SCHA for open shapes
  - SHA: function on whole unit sphere; SCHA: function on spherical cap via half-angle \theta_{c} (Figure 1)
  - SCHs widely used in geophysics (field data on planetary caps), never (to our knowledge) for geometry of patch with free edges
  - example problems:
    - topology of rough surface patch (rock surface), fractal dimension (FD)
    - different roughness regions on rocks/faults, e.g. sedimentary rocks with strata; SH (closed object) uses basis functions for all variations, no distinction of regions (multifractal surfaces)
    - matching objects by surface characteristics: medical and forensic anthropology, fractured bones or objects (cite two examples); mechanical: fragmented rocks, soil particles (cite), comparing scanned fractured regions

- What SCHA offers
  - new method for morphology of open patches with SCH, focus on nominally flat patches (global radius of curvature -> infinity)
  - any arbitrary patch, faster convergence than SHA, scales to any level of detail, reasonable computational complexity
  - reconstructing surfaces, modifying morphology of digital twins of real surfaces; useful for contact problems like friction
  - orthogonal basis -> power spectral analysis of coefficients -> fractal dimensions

- Conformal parameterisation
  - new conformal parameterisation, minimal area distortion, surface patch -> unit spherical cap
  - unique assignment per vertex, uniform distribution of features over cap
  - steps: patch -> planar disk via Choi and Lui (2015) conformal mapping (cite) + rescaling; south-pole inverse stereographic projection -> polar spherical cap; optimal Möbius transformation to minimise area distortion

- Structure
  - Sec 2 literature review; Sec 3 SCHA basis functions and solutions; Sec 4 conformal mapping; Sec 5 overall SCHA process; Sec 6 shape descriptors and FD; Sec 7 optimal \theta_{c}; Sec 8 roughness projection for microstructures; Sec 9 results; Secs 10 and 11 summary and future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the mechanics of granular materials, for example soil mechanics, the interaction of particles is investigated under various loading conditions, and the shape, size and material properties of the particles can vary a lot. Because of this, numerical models are often used to study how the mechanical behaviour of a material is influenced by the various particle morphology and the microstructures these particles create. There are similar problems in structural engineering, for example when modelling the microstructure of concrete aggregates or the various stones in stone masonry elements, since the shape and roughness of the particles affect the matrices of these materials.

To address these problems numerically, randomly shaped closed objects and their interactions have to be modelled. In these models the shape of the particle is usually represented by a finite or discrete element mesh, and the roughness of the surface is modelled with laws that describe how two surfaces interact, such as friction models. Separating the "shape" and the "roughness" of a randomly shaped particle efficiently is a challenging problem, but work in this area helps to understand the associated constitutive laws in numerical modelling better. In recent decades spherical harmonics (SH) analysis has often been used to describe the shape and roughness of stones or aggregates. This approach is transformative for closed objects, but it is difficult to apply it to the morphology of nominally flat and open surfaces (topological disks with free edges).

So in this paper we propose to use spherical cap harmonic analysis (SCHA) to describe the geometry of open shapes. The difference is that a traditional spherical harmonics analysis (SHA) describes a function mapped onto a whole unit sphere, while the SCHA describes a function mapped onto a spherical cap via a half-angle \theta_{c} (see Figure 1). SCHs are used a lot in geophysics to describe field data on planetary caps, but as far as we know they have never been used to describe the geometry of a patch with free edges. Some example problems where SCHA can be useful for the topological characterisation of a patch (i.e. an open shape with a free edge) are:

- • Studying the topology of a rough surface patch, like a rock surface, and quantifying its fractal dimension (FD).

- • Characterising different roughness regions on rocks or faults, for example sedimentary rocks made of several strata. The traditional SH approach assumes a closed object and only uses basis functions to fit all the surface variations, so it does not distinguish regions with different roughness (multifractal surfaces).

- • Matching objects based on their surface characteristics. This can be useful in medical and forensic anthropology, such as matching fractured bones or objects (see one example and another as examples), or in mechanical applications, like characterising the surfaces of fragmented rocks or soil particles by directly comparing and matching the scanned fractured regions.

- What SCHA offers
  - new method for morphology of open patches with SCH, focus on nominally flat patches (global radius of curvature -> infinity)
  - any arbitrary patch, faster convergence than SHA, scales to any level of detail, reasonable computational complexity
  - reconstructing surfaces, modifying morphology of digital twins of real surfaces; useful for contact problems like friction
  - orthogonal basis -> power spectral analysis of coefficients -> fractal dimensions

- Conformal parameterisation
  - new conformal parameterisation, minimal area distortion, surface patch -> unit spherical cap
  - unique assignment per vertex, uniform distribution of features over cap
  - steps: patch -> planar disk via Choi and Lui (2015) conformal mapping (cite) + rescaling; south-pole inverse stereographic projection -> polar spherical cap; optimal Möbius transformation to minimise area distortion

- Structure
  - Sec 2 literature review; Sec 3 SCHA basis functions and solutions; Sec 4 conformal mapping; Sec 5 overall SCHA process; Sec 6 shape descriptors and FD; Sec 7 optimal \theta_{c}; Sec 8 roughness projection for microstructures; Sec 9 results; Secs 10 and 11 summary and future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the mechanics of granular materials, for example soil mechanics, the interaction of particles is investigated under various loading conditions, and the shape, size and material properties of the particles can vary a lot. Because of this, numerical models are often used to study how the mechanical behaviour of a material is influenced by the various particle morphology and the microstructures these particles create. There are similar problems in structural engineering, for example when modelling the microstructure of concrete aggregates or the various stones in stone masonry elements, since the shape and roughness of the particles affect the matrices of these materials.

To address these problems numerically, randomly shaped closed objects and their interactions have to be modelled. In these models the shape of the particle is usually represented by a finite or discrete element mesh, and the roughness of the surface is modelled with laws that describe how two surfaces interact, such as friction models. Separating the "shape" and the "roughness" of a randomly shaped particle efficiently is a challenging problem, but work in this area helps to understand the associated constitutive laws in numerical modelling better. In recent decades spherical harmonics (SH) analysis has often been used to describe the shape and roughness of stones or aggregates. This approach is transformative for closed objects, but it is difficult to apply it to the morphology of nominally flat and open surfaces (topological disks with free edges).

So in this paper we propose to use spherical cap harmonic analysis (SCHA) to describe the geometry of open shapes. The difference is that a traditional spherical harmonics analysis (SHA) describes a function mapped onto a whole unit sphere, while the SCHA describes a function mapped onto a spherical cap via a half-angle \theta_{c} (see Figure 1). SCHs are used a lot in geophysics to describe field data on planetary caps, but as far as we know they have never been used to describe the geometry of a patch with free edges. Some example problems where SCHA can be useful for the topological characterisation of a patch (i.e. an open shape with a free edge) are:

- • Studying the topology of a rough surface patch, like a rock surface, and quantifying its fractal dimension (FD).

- • Characterising different roughness regions on rocks or faults, for example sedimentary rocks made of several strata. The traditional SH approach assumes a closed object and only uses basis functions to fit all the surface variations, so it does not distinguish regions with different roughness (multifractal surfaces).

- • Matching objects based on their surface characteristics. This can be useful in medical and forensic anthropology, such as matching fractured bones or objects (see one example and another as examples), or in mechanical applications, like characterising the surfaces of fragmented rocks or soil particles by directly comparing and matching the scanned fractured regions.

In this paper we propose a new method that uses SCH to characterise the morphology of open surface patches, and we focus specifically on nominally flat patches, for example when the global radius of the curvature of the patches approaches infinity. The SCHA method we propose lets us study the structure of any arbitrary surface patch and it converges faster than the traditional SHA, because it scales to any level of detail with reasonable computational complexity. It can also be used to reconstruct surfaces and to modify the morphology of digital twins of real surfaces, which is useful when contact problems such as friction are studied numerically. Also, because the basis functions we chose are orthogonal, we can do power spectral analyses of the coefficients from SCHA to estimate the fractal dimensions of the surfaces.

To adapt the SCHA for these applications we propose a new conformal parameterisation algorithm with minimal area distortion, which parameterises the surface patches over a unit spherical cap. The parameterisation makes sure each vertex gets a unique assignment and that the morphological features are distributed uniformly over the spherical cap. First the algorithm parameterises the surface patch to a planar disk with the conformal mapping algorithm proposed by Choi and Lui (2015), followed by a suitable rescaling. Then the disk is conformally mapped to a polar spherical cap with the south-pole inverse stereographic projection. Finally, we find an optimal Möbius transformation that minimises the area distortion on the conformal spherical cap.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 is a short literature review. Section 3 introduces the SCHA basis functions and their solutions. Section 4 describes the proposed conformal mapping algorithm and Section 5 demonstrates the overall SCHA process. Section 6 explains the shape descriptors and the derived fractal dimensions (FD). Section 7 solves the problem of finding the optimal \theta_{c} for the analysis. Section 8 explains how the morphology can be modified with a proposed roughness projection methodology for the microstructures. Section 9 shows the complete results. At the end, Sections 10 and 11 summarise the main results of the paper and discuss possible future works.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The mechanics of granular materials, such as soil mechanics, investigates the interaction of particles under various loading conditions, where the shape, size and material properties of the particles can vary widely. Numerical models are therefore often used to study how the mechanical behaviour of a material is influenced by the various particle morphology and the microstructures created by these particles. Similar problems exist in structural engineering when modelling, for example, the microstructure of concrete aggregates or the various stones in stone masonry elements, since the shape and roughness of the particles affect the matrices of these materials.

Addressing these problems numerically requires modelling randomly shaped closed objects and their interactions. In such models, the shape of the particle is typically represented by a finite or discrete element mesh, while the roughness of the surface is modelled through laws describing the interaction of two surfaces, such as friction models. Efficiently separating "shape" and "roughness" of a randomly shaped particle is a challenging problem, though work in this area helps us better understand the associated constitutive laws in numerical modelling. In recent decades, spherical harmonics (SH) analysis has frequently been used to describe the shape and roughness of stones or aggregates. However, while this approach is transformative for closed objects, it is difficult to apply to the morphology of nominally flat and open surfaces (topological disks with free edges). In this paper, we therefore propose using spherical cap harmonic analysis (SCHA) to describe the geometry of open shapes. The difference is that while a traditional spherical harmonics analysis (SHA) describes a function mapped onto an entire unit sphere, the SCHA describes a function mapped onto a spherical cap via a half-angle \theta_{c} (see Figure 1). SCHs are widely used in geophysics to describe field data on planetary caps, but to our knowledge have never been used to describe the geometry of a patch with free edges. Here we give example problems where SCHA can be useful for the topological characterisation of a patch (i.e. an open shape with a free edge):

- • For studying the topology of a rough surface patch, such as a rock surface, and quantifying its fractal dimension (FD).

- • For characterising different roughness regions on rocks or faults, such as sedimentary rocks made of several strata. The traditional SH approach, which assumes a closed object, only uses basis functions to fit all the surface variations and does not distinguish regions of different roughness (multifractal surfaces).

- • For matching objects based on surface characteristics. This can be useful for medical and forensic anthropology applications, such as matching fractured bones or objects (see [1] and [2] as examples), or for mechanical applications, such as characterising the surfaces of fragmented rocks or soil particles [3,4] by directly comparing and matching the scanned fractured regions.

In this paper, we propose a new method for characterising the morphology of open surface patches using SCH, focusing specifically on nominally flat patches, such as when the global radius of the curvature of the targeted patches approaches infinity. The proposed SCHA method allows us to study the structure of any arbitrary surface patch with faster convergence than the traditional SHA, as it scales to any level of detail with reasonable computational complexity. It can also be used for reconstructing surfaces and modifying the morphology of digital twins of real surfaces, which is useful when numerically studying contact problems such as friction. In addition, the chosen orthogonal basis functions allow us to conduct power spectral analyses of the coefficients obtained from SCHA to estimate the fractal dimensions of the surfaces.

To adapt the SCHA for these applications, we propose a new conformal parameterisation algorithm with minimal area distortion for parameterising the surface patches over a unit spherical cap. The parameterisation ensures a unique assignment for each vertex and a uniform distribution of the morphological features over the spherical cap. First, the algorithm parameterises the surface patch to a planar disk using the conformal mapping algorithm proposed by Choi and Lui (2015) [5], followed by a suitable rescaling. Then, using the south-pole inverse stereographic projection, we conformally map the disk to a polar spherical cap. Finally, we find an optimal Möbius transformation to minimise the area distortion on the conformal spherical cap.

This paper is structured as follows: Section 2 gives a brief literature review. We then introduce the SCHA basis functions and their solutions in Section 3. In Section 4, we describe the proposed conformal mapping algorithm and then demonstrate the overall SCHA process in Section 5. Next, we explain the shape descriptors and the derived fractal dimensions (FD) in Section 6. In Section 7 we solve the problem of finding the optimal \theta_{c} for the analysis. In Section 8, we explain how to modify the morphology with a proposed roughness projection methodology for the microstructures. The complete results are shown in Section 9. Finally, we summarise the main results of the paper and discuss possible future works in Sections 10 and 11, respectively.

References:
[1] National Institute of Justice, Reconstructing fragmentary skeletal remains, ( February 2017).
[2] C. Jia, L. He, X. Yang, X. Han, B. Chang, X. Han, Developing a reassembling algorithm for broken objects, IEEE Access 8 (2020) 220320–220334.
[3] M. Wu, J. J. Wang, An investigation of 3D sand particle fragment reassembly, in: Micro to MACRO Mathematical Modelling in Soil Mechanics, Springer, 2018, pp. 383–390.
[4] M. Wu, J. Wang, Registration of point cloud data for matching crushed sand particles, Powder Technology 347 (2019) 227–242.
[5] P. T. Choi, L. M. Lui, Fast disk conformal parameterization of simply-connected open surfaces, Journal of Scientific Computing 65 (3) (2015) 1065–1090.
